sections.overview: The red-backed shrike is a small songbird that hunts like a bird of prey from perches and impales its catches on thorns. It breeds across much of Europe and migrates to southern Africa, but has almost vanished as a breeding bird in Britain.
sections.identification: A little larger but slimmer than a house sparrow, an adult weighs about 28 g with a wing near 95 mm. The male has a bluish-grey head, a black mask, a bright chestnut back and a thick black bill. Shrikes typically perch in the open.
sections.habitat: It favours semi-open landscapes with hedges and thorny bushes beside insect-rich grassland, ideally sunny places with short or bare ground where prey can be reached. In Sweden, territories were small, about 0.5–1 hectare, with plenty of well-spread perches.
sections.diet: Its prey is mostly small and medium-sized insects, which are also what the chicks are fed, together with some small vertebrates. Shrikes take their catches to a larder, where they impale them on a thorn or wedge them into branches to store them for later.
sections.behavior: Shrikes watch for prey from the tops of bushes, fence posts and wires. The red-backed shrike is a long-distance migrant: late-spring arrivals may wait for food to become available in the African wet season before crossing the Sahara. In Britain it is now a scarce passage visitor, mostly in May–June and August–October.
sections.reproduction: A clutch is typically four to six eggs, incubated by the female for about 14 days. The chicks hatch naked and fledge at 14–15 days. There is usually one brood a season, occasionally two. Nests are placed low in thorny shrubs; in a Turkish study blackberry was the most common nest site.
sections.ecology: The shrike depends on thorny cover and insect-rich open ground close together. Nest predation was the main cause of nest failure in a study in northern Turkey. Intensive farming that removes insect-rich grassland next to hedges is expected to cause long-term declines.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide. In the UK it is Red-listed and legally protected, with about three breeding pairs in 2013–17 after it became effectively extinct as a breeder in 1989. Its British breeding range contracted by 88% between 1968–72 and 2008–11.
